newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban conquer opposition stronghold.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban conquer opposition stronghold.

text.p: The Taleban Islamic militia entered the main northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Saturday with little fighting, hours after its reported capture of another opposition stronghold.

Groups of Taleban fighters, waving white flags from tanks and jeeps, rode into the former stronghold of opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum at 5 p.m. (1230 gmt) amid bursts of celebratory gunfire.

A Reuter correspondent in the Afghan capital Kabul quoted an Afghan source in Mazar-i-Sharif as saying there was some fighting on the outskirts of the city but that he had seen no bodies in the streets.
Taleban fighters were shooting at portraits of Dostum which stand at city road junctions, the source said.
It was not immediately clear how the Taleban managed to enter the city, which had been well guarded by Dostum's troops.
The Taleban fighters entered Mazar-i-Sharif, capital of Balkh province, hours after Taleban sources reported the fall of Dostum's military headquarters town of Shibarghan, capital of Jozjan province.
Earlier, panic swept Mazar-i-Sharif after reports of the fall of Shibarghan, 130 km (80 miles) to the west.
Shopkeepers pulled down their shutters, soldiers fled in tanks and security men roughed up foreign cameramen, witnesses said. Some soldiers stole cars.
Streets emptied as people raced to get home, and witnesses said some were trying to flee north towards the border with Uzbekistan.
There was no immediate confirmation of the fall of Shibarghan and no word on Dostum's whereabouts.

Sources in the Taleban Islamic movement, quoted by a Pakistan-based private Afghan news service, said Shibarghan was captured by anti-Dostum forces led by Taleban leader Abdul Razzaq, governor of the western province of Herat.
The report came hours after three jet fighters of Dostum's air force defected to his opponents, and only a day after Western reporters drove to Shibarghan from Mazar-i-Sharif to find it calm.
The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) agency also said defectors later flew another jet and two helicopters to the Taleban side.

A defecting officer of Dostum's air force, Major General Yussef Shah, told reporters in Kabul he made the 35-minute flight in his L39 Albatross trainer from Shibarghan airport to the capital because he feared that Dostum was trying to split Afghanistan.
Two Soviet-built Su-22 fighter bombers were earlier flown from Shibarghan to Maimana, capital of Faryab province, he said.
"We feared that Dostum was trying to dismantle Afghanistan. More planes are expected to come over," said Yussef, clean-shaven and wearing combat fatigues.
Maimana is held by Dostum's former foreign minister and deputy, General Abdul Malik, who launched a revolt against Dostum on Monday.
"One of the pilots was Colonel General Hafeez, the head of (Dostum's) air force. They bombed Shibarghan air base on their way out," said Yussef.
"Dostum had four Su-22s, three MiG-21s, and four L39s before today, now he has lost three of them," he said.
Yussef said the Taleban and their new ally General Malik now faced Dostum's forces on a front line some 15 km (nine miles) from Shibarghan.
He said Dostum's forces still held the town of Sar-i-Pul, but that Taleban forces were within two km (1-1/4 miles) of it.

The opposition alliance led by Dostum, who has led the fight against the purist Islamic Taleban, was thrown into disarray by Malik's revolt, which broke an 18-month deadlock on the front line in Badghis province.
The Taleban, who seized Kabul last September and control most of Afghanistan, now command all of Badghis and its eastern neighbour Faryab and are making inroads into Sar-i-Pul province.
